summary.text: Voyager 1 is a NASA space probe launched on September 5, 1977, to study the outer Solar System and the interstellar space beyond the Sun's heliosphere.
It flew past Jupiter, Saturn and Saturn's largest moon, Titan, and crossed the heliopause into interstellar space on August 25, 2012, the first spacecraft to do so.
As of October 2026 it is the most distant human-made object from Earth, at 172.52 AU.

items.prompt: NASA could send the probe past Pluto or past Titan, not both. Why did Titan get priority?

options.label: Pluto had already been photographed by another probe
Titan was known to have a substantial atmosphere
Titan sat directly on the route to Saturn's rings
Pluto was known to have no moons worth studying

items.explain: Exploration of Titan took priority because it was known to have a substantial atmosphere.

items.prompt: Which boundary did Voyager 1 cross on August 25, 2012, to enter interstellar space?

options.label: The heliopause
The orbit of Saturn
The edge of the Kuiper belt
The Van Allen radiation belts

items.explain: Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause and became the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space.

items.prompt: Voyager 1 is billions of kilometres away. Through what does Earth send it routine commands and receive its data?

options.label: A chain of relay satellites around Jupiter
Home television dishes pointed at the Sun
A radio station built on the Moon
The NASA Deep Space Network

items.explain: Voyager 1 communicates through the NASA Deep Space Network to receive routine commands and transmit data.

items.prompt: What makes the radioisotope generators on Voyager 1 produce less power as the years pass?

options.label: The fuel decays slowly and the thermocouples degrade
Dust builds up and blocks sunlight from reaching them
Cold space drains the plutonium faster than expected
The thrusters pull power away from them

items.explain: Their power output declines because of the fuel's 87.7-year half-life and degradation of the thermocouples.

items.prompt: Why was the mission renamed Voyager after first being called Mariner Jupiter-Saturn?

options.label: NASA cut the budget and dropped the Mariner program
The name honoured the moons of Jupiter and Saturn
The probe designs began to differ greatly from Mariner missions
A new laboratory took over building the probes

items.explain: The name changed to Voyager when the probe designs began to differ substantially from Mariner missions. The budget cuts had led to the earlier Mariner Jupiter-Saturn name.

items.prompt: Engineers fired Voyager 1's trajectory correction thrusters for the first time since 1980. What did that gain the mission?

options.label: It restored every instrument to working order
It doubled the probe's speed away from the Sun
It turned the probe back toward the planets
It extended the mission by two to three years

items.explain: Firing the thrusters in 2017 enabled the mission to be extended by two to three years.

paragraphs.heading: The farthest spacecraft
paragraphs.text: Voyager 1 is a NASA space probe launched on September 5, 1977, 16 days after its twin, Voyager 2. It was sent to study the outer Solar System and then the interstellar space beyond the Sun's heliosphere. As of October 2026 it is 172.52 AU, or about 25.8 billion km, away. No other object made by people is farther from Earth.

paragraphs.heading: Jupiter, Saturn and Titan
paragraphs.text: On its way out it flew past Jupiter, Saturn and Titan, Saturn's largest moon. NASA had to choose between a flyby of Pluto or one of Titan. Titan won because it was known to have a substantial atmosphere. The probe looked at the weather, rings and magnetic fields of both gas giants, and it was the first probe to send back detailed pictures of their moons.

paragraphs.heading: Into interstellar space
paragraphs.text: Its extended mission, shared with Voyager 2, is to find and study the outer edges of the heliosphere and to start exploring the interstellar medium. On August 25, 2012, Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause and became the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space. Two years later the Sun's coronal mass ejections hit it in a third wave that lasted until at least December 15, 2014. That gave more evidence that it really was in interstellar space.

paragraphs.heading: How it is built
paragraphs.text: Voyager 1 was built by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Its main body is a ten-sided prism. It carries 11 science instruments, plus 16 hydrazine thrusters and gyroscopes that help keep its radio antenna pointed at Earth. That antenna is a 3.7-meter dish that sends and receives radio waves through the three Deep Space Network stations on Earth. Power comes from three radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) filled with plutonium-238, which made about 470 W at launch.

paragraphs.heading: Running down slowly
paragraphs.text: By 2025 its signals took more than 23 hours to reach Earth, and it is projected to reach one light day from Earth on November 18, 2026. The power from its RTGs drops over time as the fuel decays and the thermocouples wear out. As of 2026 only two instruments still work: the Plasma Wave Subsystem and the magnetometer. The RTGs may give enough power to send engineering data until 2036.

paragraphs.heading: Reviving old thrusters
paragraphs.text: In 2017 the team fired the spacecraft's trajectory correction thrusters for the first time since 1980, which let the mission run two to three years longer. Several more thrusters were brought back into use in 2018, 2019 and 2025. The extended mission is expected to keep returning science for several more years.
